newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left set for big gains in 1998-poll.
newsitem.headline: French left set for big gains in 1998-poll.

text.p: France's leftist opposition parties are set for big gains in legislative elections in 1998, helped by disaffection with conservative President Jacques Chirac and rising unemployment, an opinion poll showed on Tuesday.

The Sofres survey, for the Nouvel Observateur weekly, showed that 40 percent of voters intended to vote for the Socialists or Communist parties on the first round of the elections due in March 1998, up from 28.1 percent in 1993.

The poll, of 1,000 people from December 21-24, indicated that support for the ruling Rally for the Republic (RPR) and Union for French Democracy (UDF) parties would slip to 34 percent from 39.9 percent.

The survey did not predict the overall winner under the complicated two-stage vote, but indicated that 45 percent of voters favoured a victory by the Socialists and their allies, up from 37 percent in a similar poll a year ago.
If elected, the Socialists have promised to cut working hours and create 700,000 jobs for the young within two years without widening the budget deficit.
Thirty-three percent of those polled wanted a victory by parties in the ruling centre-right, down from 38 percent a year ago. Twenty-two percent had no opinion.

A Socialist win would force Chirac, elected for seven years in 1995, into "cohabitation" with a leftist cabinet. Chirac's predecessor, the late Socialist Francois Mitterrand, twice co-habited with the centre-right during 14 years in office.
Chirac was due to make a New Year address later on Tuesday in a bid to revive optimism in France despite record unemployment of 12.7 percent.
The Socialists were themselves routed in the last legislative elections in 1993, hit by rising unemployment and creeping sleaze scandals.
